newsitem.title: POLAND: Persistent rain threatens return of Polish floods.
newsitem.headline: Persistent rain threatens return of Polish floods.

text.p: Poland, still reeling from disastrous floods earlier this month, endured more rain in some areas on Saturday.

"The situation isn't good. Rain is falling intensively in Silesia, rivers are rising, and probably the flood will be repeated," Krzysztof Pomes, spokesman for the government's crisis committee, said on Saturday morning.
He said eight provinces of the south and west were on flood alert although in some places the downpours were less intense and rivers were rising more slowly than than initially expected.
"It started raining yesterday and should rain rather intensively today," Pomes said. The key questions were: how much would fall and where?

The uneven intensity of the rain gave some hope that Poland might be spared a full return of the floods that claimed 49 lives, swamped 4,000 sq km (1,500 sq miles) and affected about 1,000 communities, including the major cities of Wroclaw and Opole.

But some towns and villages were already being plunged back into the nightmare. Several villages in Zielona Gora province were told to evacuate after a dyke broke. Some streets of the lower Silesia mining town of Walbrzych were again under water.

Bitter experience meant that this time the government and hundreds of thousands of Poles in affected areas were taking few chances. Thousands of troops were helping citizens build sandbag barriers and strengthened weakened dykes.

In Opole on the river Odra, where two metres of water raged around high-rise city-centre buildings last week, authorities told citizens to listen for three-minute siren warnings -- after which they would have an hour to reach evacuation points.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, accused by the opposition for failing to reassure people and mobilise effective action at the start of the deluge, broadcast to the nation on television late on Friday to set out aid measures.

Apart from seeing through parliament new laws, including ones allowing higher government borrowing and giving handouts to devastated households, the government has deployed more than 20,000 troops and set up an emergency communications system to replace one that failed last time.

Parliament also hastily amended the communist-era state of emergency law, removing the most draconian provisions so it could be applied in case of further floods for such reasons as to fight looting or freeze prices to stop profiteering.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski signed the amended law but said he would not declare an emergency unless the disaster resumed in full, PAP news agency reported.
The opposition wants a state of emergency now, although this would delay parliamentary elections due on September 21 as polls cannot be held within three months of an emergency.

"If it turns out we are really dealing with a second flood wave, hitting more regions, then a state of emergency and a delay in the elections could happen," PAP news agency quoted Kwasniewski as saying late on Friday.
The elections will pit the ruling ex-communists against a strong alliance built around the Solidarity trade union, which is strongly critical of the government's crisis-management.
Cimoszewicz has said his administration acted effectively, given that the vast scale of the floods was totally unexpected.
The crisis has shaken Poland's zloty currency, forcing the central bank on Friday to sell dollars to defend it.
